title: Russia's Fuel Crisis Deepens as Drone Strikes Slash Refinery Output by 40%
excerpt: Moscow diverts Siberian fuel and imports gasoline from India as Ukrainian attacks leave production at 65% of seasonal demand, with Crimea under rationing and farmers squeezed by soaring diesel costs.
body:
Russian authorities are redirecting fuel supplies from Siberia and ramping up imports from Belarus and India to prevent shortages in the Moscow region, as Ukrainian drone attacks on oil refineries have driven the country's worst fuel crisis in decades, according to Reuters.

Gasoline output fell to around 65% of average seasonal consumption in early July after undershooting demand for several months. The crunch has been felt across all 11 time zones since May, when Ukraine escalated strikes on refineries to undermine the Russian war effort.

Moscow Shielded, Periphery Suffers

An attack on the Moscow Oil Refinery in mid-June caused fuel shortages and long queues at filling stations. By mid-July, supplies in the Moscow region — home to 22 million people — stabilized after the Achinsk refinery in Siberia's Krasnoyarsk region and others redirected output to the capital. Traders estimated the additional supplies at several hundred thousand metric tons.

The Moscow region consumes around 6 million tons of gasoline per year. Russia has also started importing refined fuel from India — a reversal for one of the world's top energy exporters.

"Farmers are losing around 1,000 roubles ($12.70) per metric ton of grain due to rising diesel prices, according to Andrey Sizov of the SovEcon consultancy."

"The authorities conceal information about the actual scale of the attacks and, at the same time, artificially keep gasoline prices low, which creates explosive demand and leads to shortages."

— Andrei Yakovlev, Free University of Berlin

Crimea is the worst-affected region, with fuel rationing, suspended children's tourism activities, and shorter hours for shops and cafes. Elsewhere, some regions have limited sales to 20-30 liters per vehicle, with wait times stretching past five hours.

Economic Fallout Mounting

Refining capacity has been cut by roughly 40%, according to Andrei Yakovlev. The government has imposed QR-code purchase restrictions and license plate tracking — half-measures economists say risk fueling a black market.

The crisis is crushing Russian agriculture. Farmers are losing around 1,000 roubles ($12.70) per metric ton of grain due to rising diesel prices, according to Andrey Sizov of the SovEcon consultancy. Russia exported 61 million tons of grain last year; Sizov warned it could fall short by 5 to 10 million tons of wheat if Sea of Azov shipping restrictions persist.

"If there is no military solution to open up the Sea of Azov, and the situation drags on for most of the second half of the year, Russia could fall short of supplying the global market by 5 to 10 million tons of wheat."

— Andrey Sizov, SovEcon

The broader economy is fraying. Around 500,000 Russian SMEs went bankrupt in 2025 — a third more than the prior year — and 10% of corporate loans are non-performing, according to a European intelligence report cited by Reuters.

Global Ripple Effects and India's Energy Calculus

Russia's diesel export ban has pushed European diesel refining margins to a record above $60 per barrel, according to Saxo Bank. Morgan Stanley projects European diesel inventories will fall to multi-year lows by year-end.

For India, the dynamics cut both ways. Indian refiners imported a record 2.64 million barrels per day of Russian crude in June — worth $5.14 billion — with Russian oil now accounting for 41% of India's import mix, up from 38% a year ago, according to Reuters data. India has become Russia's second-largest fossil fuel buyer. India has also hiked export taxes on diesel and jet fuel in response to tight global markets.

What's Next

Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the domestic fuel market had partly stabilized, but economists see no quick fix. Refining output will likely take months, if not years, to recover — assuming no further Ukrainian strikes, an assumption few are willing to make. Brussels is preparing a 21st sanctions package targeting Russian banks, which could further strain the economy. With global fuel stocks running thin, the squeeze on Russian consumers and world energy markets looks set to intensify through 2026.
